title: The radio show and the shrinking band
summary: The Whiteman band was now on radio with Roy Bargy in front, records weren't selling, and the band shrank for the summer.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Well, at this time, you know, there's another thing. We're not making many records, we're doing a radio show and this is 18 to 20 numbers patterned after the Lucky Strike, B. A. Rolfe thing, this is 16, 18, 20 numbers an hour and you had to have the cuts, you had everything marked and at your rehearsal, which Roy was now in front of the band --

Roy Barbey had the band. Whiteman is in the studio, and -- in the control room -- and it's not a good situation for the band, as it as, when we were all happy. We're not making many records. Particularly because they're not selling. Nobody's records are selling at this time.

This was a new low in record sales and it was not a good situation, so when this comes, I could see it. Everybody else could see it and it was -- the Whiteman band had been lucky for the previous two years to have had these -- to have had that moving picture contract, the Old Gold contract and the contract for the theatres. The theatre contract.
So which was Paramount Republics. Now this -- So the only thing to do is cut down the band. I'm surprised

he even did this. But he cut down the band, he had a job up or someplace up there, in Pelham Heath, or up in the Pelham Parkway for the summer, so he cut the band down to 16 pieces and it was not long after that even Grote got out of there. I think Grote -- it was maybe around that time, I don't know. I don't remember.

But I know eight of us got out at the time and the Rhythm Boys had not come back with the band, so that they only had the other trio and it was getting down with whatever bands were around, big bands, were around at that time, so that he was entering a new phase with his band.
